column4: The section identifies رحم as both womb and child-home; this verse says God forms people in الْأَرْحَامِ as He wills, making the lexical image an explicit Qur'anic scene.
The section labels kinship a borrowed use of رحم because relatives come from one womb; this verse places الْأَرْحَامَ beside reverence for God, making that bond an ethical charge.
This command extends worship of God to doing good to parents; the next ayah, 17:24, names their raising of the speaker as a child and completes the section's parent-care image.
This joins the section's roots ر ح م and ر ب ب: show parents humility “from mercy” and ask for mercy as they raised the speaker small, making upbringing the ground of reciprocal care.
Imran's wife dedicates what is in her womb to God; the child is already held within a vowed relation before birth, like the section's womb as a child's vessel and home.
After the birth, the mother asks God to protect Mary and her descendants from Satan; this gives the section's child-home image its concrete maternal act of protection.
Mary is made to grow with a good growth, placed in Zakariya's care, and given provision; this directly stages nurture, a non-birth caregiver, and sustenance together.
Moses' mother is told to nurse him and then set him in the river if she fears for him; the verse stages infant nurture and the painful separation that the section's womb-to-home image implies.
Pharaoh's people take up the infant Moses; this is the next handoff in the child-care scene, before Pharaoh's wife asks that he be spared in 28:9.
Pharaoh's wife calls Moses a comfort to her eyes and proposes taking him as a son; this is an explicit household receiving and cherishing a child born elsewhere.
Moses' mother is left with an empty heart after the separation; this gives the section's account of the mother's bond its cost before the child is returned.
Moses' sister follows him from afar; this is a specific act of watchful care between the mother's loss and her offer of a foster household in 28:12.
Moses' sister offers a household who will care for him (يَكْفُلُونَهُ); this directly meets the section's dictionary sense of ر ب ب for a foster parent taking responsibility for a child.
God returns Moses to his mother so her eye may be comforted; the birth mother's home and the nursing bond are restored after foster care.
Moses reaches full strength and maturity and is given judgment and knowledge; this is the completion point for the section's growth “from state to state.”
God recalls revealing to Moses' mother; 20:39 continues with the infant placed in the chest and raised under God's eye, completing the mother's role in the same childhood scene.
Moses is placed in the chest and God says he would be raised عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي; this makes divine oversight an explicit counterpart to the section's care that carries a child through danger.
Moses' sister offers someone who will وَكَفَلَهُ and God returns him to his mother; the verse connects foster care and the restored maternal home in one account.
Zakariya asks for good offspring after seeing Mary's provision and care; the scene ties a desired child to the household nurture just shown in 3:37.
Zakariya receives the news of Yahya while standing in prayer; this is the answer to his request for offspring in 3:38 and continues the child-given-by-God scene.
Zakariya asks how he can have a boy in old age while his wife is barren; the verse makes the bodily limits around childbearing explicit.
Zakariya asks not to be left without a child; this directly concerns the household's continuation through offspring.
God answers Zakariya's prayer and heals his wife, while the family hastens to good and calls with hope and fear; this joins childbearing and sustained devotion.
Sarah is given the news of Isaac and then Jacob; the verse presents offspring entering an older couple's household.
Sarah wonders how she can bear a child in old age; 11:71 gives the news and 11:73 names mercy and blessing on the household, framing the bodily surprise.
The visitors name Allah's mercy and blessing upon Abraham's household (أَهْلَ الْبَيْتِ); this directly joins ر ح م to a family home and the promised child.
The passage is introduced as the Lord's mercy to Zakariya, whose prayer for offspring follows; here mercy is told through a childless household's appeal.
Zakariya fears what his kin will do after him and says his wife is barren; the prayer for an heir places family continuity and childbearing together.
Zakariya is given the good news of Yahya; the next ayah, 19:8, spells out the old age and barrenness that make this birth striking.
Zakariya asks how he can have a boy when his wife is barren and he is advanced in age; the verse directly marks the limits surrounding gestation and parenthood.
Yahya is given tenderness from God (حَنَانًا) and purity; this is a specific form of the tender care that the section says moves mercy toward the one receiving it.
Yahya is dutiful to his parents and not arrogant; the verse shows the reciprocal family good that the section develops from parental upbringing and mercy.
Human creation begins from an extract of clay; 23:13 moves the created seed into a secure lodging, starting the section's movement from origin toward completion.
The human seed is placed in a secure lodging (قَرَارٍ مَّكِينٍ); 23:14 continues its formation stage by stage, making the womb a protected place of growth.
The verse recounts successive formation and a later created form; it gives a concrete bodily sequence for the section's definition of تربِيَة as bringing something through states to completion.
This passage moves from drop and clot through formation in the womb to birth as an infant and maturity; it most fully stages the section's home, successive growth, and completion.
God creates people in their mothers' wombs, “creation after creation,” within three darknesses; the verse combines the womb-home and successive formation.
God knows what each female bears and what wombs diminish or increase; this makes the child's hidden growth and its measure part of the section's womb image.
The verse traces a person from dust and drop through clot, infancy, maturity, and old age; it gives a full life-stage counterpart to growth toward completion.
The verse says God created people in successive stages (أَطْوَارًا); this is a direct formulation of the section's “state by state” account of nurture.
A mother carries and delivers in hardship, while gestation and weaning take thirty months before a person reaches full strength; this spans womb, care, and maturity.
The verse recalls a mother carrying her child in weakness upon weakness and weaning him over two years, joining maternal cost to the child's dependent growth.
People come from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing and are given hearing, sight, and hearts; the verse continues development from birth into capacities for learning.
Mothers nurse children for two full years and the father is responsible for provision and clothing; this makes the household's practical work of feeding and supporting a child explicit.
The verse requires housing pregnant women through birth and payment if they nurse the child; it shows care continuing through childbirth and into paid nursing, including care across households.
Spending is measured by what each person has, with hardship followed by ease; 65:6 supplies the concrete housing and nursing duties this rule supports.
Guardians test orphans until they reach marriageable maturity, then hand over their property; this directly connects protection and responsible care to a child's growth into adulthood.
The treasure is kept for two orphan boys until they mature because their father was righteous; this makes protection during childhood an effect of a parent's care that outlasts his life.
The verse names stepdaughters in one's care (رَبَائِبُكُمُ اللَّاتِي فِي حُجُورِكُم); this directly matches the section's dictionary entry ر ب ب for a step-parent who undertakes a child's upbringing.

The verse calls people رَبَّانِيِّينَ because they teach the Scripture and study it; it directly connects the section's root ر ب ب, whose teaching sense is feeding learners small portions of knowledge, to instruction.
This ayah names the All-Merciful (الرَّحْمَٰنُ); 55:2 immediately presents Him teaching the Qur'an, as in the section's cited sequence of mercy and instruction.
The All-Merciful teaches the Qur'an; this is the teaching act the section uses to extend nurture beyond bodily growth.
Human creation follows the teaching of the Qur'an and precedes teaching expression in this passage; the section's cited sequence makes human formation part of the teaching scene.
God teaches the human being expression; this is a direct parallel to the section's extension of nurture into instruction.
The human is created from a clinging clot; this names an early bodily stage, while 96:4–5 turns to the teaching that develops what a person can know.
God teaches by the pen; 96:5 completes the claim by saying He teaches the human what was unknown, paralleling the section's small-knowledge-to-learning branch.
God teaches the human what he did not know; this concretely matches the section's dictionary sense of a teacher feeding learners knowledge.
Human life moves from weakness to strength and back to weakness; this is a specific sequence of states that illuminates the section's growth-through-stages definition.
A human begins as a drop of emitted fluid; 75:38–39 continues through clot and formation, so this row supplies the first stage of a distinct development sequence.
The emitted drop becomes a clot before God forms and proportions the human in 75:39; the sequence concretizes successive formation.
God forms and proportions the human and makes the two sexes; this completes the sequence that began with the drop in 75:37.
God gives spouses, children, grandchildren, and good provision; this directly joins household growth to the sustenance named in the section's provision branch.
The verse says God made human beings from fluid and made kinship and marriage ties; it joins bodily generation to the family relations the section traces to one womb.
The prayer asks for spouses and offspring who are a comfort to the eyes and for the family to lead the righteous; this makes care, joy, and moral upbringing a household aspiration.
God places affection and mercy (مَوَدَّةً وَرَحْمَةً) between spouses; this gives the section's Rahman/Rahim frame a concrete household relation.
Abraham asks God to provide fruit for his family left in a barren valley; this concretely joins the section's household and its dictionary branch غ ي ر, provision brought home.

Joseph's brothers say they will bring provisions for their household (نَمِيرُ أَهْلَنَا); this is a direct Qur'anic counterpart to the section's dictionary gloss of الغِيرة as المِيرة, provisions for the home.
The verse presents milk from livestock as a drink; this is a specific provision parallel to the section's dictionary image of a sheep kept at home for milk.
The verse names milk and other benefits from livestock; this parallels the section's domestic sheep kept for milk, while widening the provision image to a herd.
The section's root ق و م includes household support (قِوَام); here wealth is called قِيَامًا لِّلنَّاس, what sustains people's affairs, linking material means to a household's standing.
The section's ق و م dictionary sense is sustaining a household; this verse calls men قَوَّامُونَ over women and explicitly ties that role to spending from their wealth.
The command to maintain prayer and enjoin it on one's family makes household stewardship an ongoing responsibility, a concrete form of keeping the household's affairs standing.
Believers are told to protect themselves and their families from the Fire; this directly meets the section's dictionary branch غَيْرَة as protective concern for one's household.
The verse requires permission before entering other people's homes; this marks the home as a protected boundary, matching the section's household-protection sense of غَيْرَة.
Children and household dependents must seek permission at three private times; the rule makes care for a household include protecting its intimate spaces.
When children reach puberty they must ask permission like adults; the verse stages a change in household care as the child matures.
The verse commands good treatment of parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy; this concretely enacts the section's definition of رحمة as tenderness that leads to good for the vulnerable.
The covenant requires good treatment of parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy; these are the family and vulnerable recipients specified by the section's mercy gloss.
God commands good (الْإِحْسَانِ) and giving to near kin; this directly joins the section's mercy-that-leads-to-good definition with its kinship branch of ر ح م.
The verse tells people to give the relative his due; this turns the section's womb-derived kinship into a concrete obligation of support.
Blood relatives are declared closer to one another in God's decree; this gives the section's womb-based account of kinship a concrete legal consequence.
The verse condemns severing ties of kinship (أَرْحَامَكُمْ); it marks the boundary opposite to the section's account of relatives joined through one womb.
Virtue includes giving wealth to relatives, orphans, and the needy; this makes mercy toward kin and the vulnerable a concrete practice rather than only a feeling.
Asked what to spend, the verse names parents, relatives, orphans, and the needy; it specifies how household provision can extend to vulnerable kin.
The verse says reforming the affairs of orphans is best and that sharing life with them is like kinship; this is direct guidance for caring for vulnerable children.
The righteous give food, despite their own desire for it, to the needy, orphan, and captive; this concretely enacts mercy as beneficence toward the weak.
The passage names feeding in a day of hunger; 90:15–17 specifies the vulnerable recipients and frames this as a path of mercy.
The hungry-day passage specifies an orphan who is near of kin; it joins vulnerability and kinship, two recipients named in the section's mercy account.
The passage adds a poor person in the dust; 90:17 completes the sequence by urging mutual patience and mercy.
The verse urges people to counsel one another to mercy (مَرْحَمَة); the preceding ayat show that mercy as feeding an orphan and a poor person.
God recalls finding the Prophet an orphan and giving him shelter; this is an explicit instance of a vulnerable child received into protection.
The verse forbids overpowering or mistreating an orphan; it draws a direct boundary around the weak child named in the section's mercy gloss.
The verse forbids repelling the asker; it turns tenderness toward a vulnerable person into a concrete restraint on conduct.
The verse says a person mistakes expanded provision and comfort (نَعَّمَهُ) for proof of honor; 89:17–18 overturn that measure by asking whether the orphan is honored and the poor fed.
The person mistakes restricted provision for humiliation; 89:17–18 name care for the orphan and hungry as the real test, reversing the comfort measure linked to the section's root ن ع م.
The verse rebukes failure to honor the orphan; this reverses the section's mercy toward the weak and shows comfort alone is not good upbringing.
The verse rebukes failure to urge feeding the poor; it reverses the section's household provision and mercy toward the vulnerable.
The verse condemns consuming inheritance without restraint; it marks a family boundary against turning household resources away from rightful care.
The verse condemns excessive love of wealth after the rebukes about orphans and feeding; it sets possession against the section's mercy expressed in provision.
The verse describes pushing away the orphan; this is a specific reversal of the section's tenderness and good action toward the weak.
The verse describes failing to urge the feeding of the needy; it reverses the section's mercy as practical beneficence.
Those who consume orphan property unjustly are said to consume fire; this marks a concrete opposite to the section's care for vulnerable children and their household provision.
The verse forbids killing children because of poverty and promises provision for parents and children; it reverses the protection and household support developed in the section.
The verse forbids killing children from fear of poverty and promises provision for them and their parents; it gives the section's child-care image a boundary against fear-driven abandonment.
The verse says adopted sons are not one's biological sons; this marks a boundary between the section's foster-parent role and lineage.
The verse says to call adopted children by their fathers' names when known; it clarifies that raising a child in a home does not erase the lineage distinction.
Pharaoh says he raised Moses as a child (نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا); as the section explains, this is a partial claim beside Moses' nursing by his mother and being brought up under God's eye.
In the waiting-period rule, women must not conceal what God created in their wombs; this gives رحم a concrete household and lineage consequence, beyond the womb as a place of formation.
The passage moves from a pair to pregnancy that grows heavy and a prayer for a sound child; it directly stages gestation and dependence on God for offspring.

The next ayah reverses the prayer for a sound child by describing partners being assigned after the child is granted; the couple is unnamed, but the immediate scene sets childbearing under God's gift rather than parental control.
God is said to grant daughters or sons as He wills; this makes offspring in the household a gift of the One who governs the womb and its outcomes.
The passage adds mixed offspring or barrenness to God's gifts and limits; this completes its account of how households receive children.
Zakariya says his bones have weakened and his head is gray while asking for a child; this makes the bodily cost of late parenthood explicit.
Zakariya asks for a child to inherit him and the family of Jacob; this directly joins offspring to continuity of the kinship household.
Yahya is told to hold Scripture firmly while still a boy and is given judgment; this is a specific instance of instruction as formative nurture.
After Mary's labor, a voice tells her not to grieve and points to a stream beneath her; this continues the childbirth scene with immediate care and provision.
The verse says God's mercy made the Prophet gentle toward his companions; this concretely shows the section's ر ح م as tenderness that benefits its recipients.
The Prophet is described as deeply concerned for believers and رَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ toward them; this gives the section's mercy-to-the-weak a specific communal form.
The Prophet is told to lower his wing to the believers; this repeats the section's image of humble, protective care from 17:24 in a community setting.
The Prophet is told to lower his wing to the believers who follow him; this repeats the section's concrete posture of merciful humility.
Luqman begins instructing his son against associating partners with God; this makes the parent's work of forming a child through teaching explicit.
The son must not obey parents who urge shirk, yet must accompany them kindly in this life; this gives parent-child care a specific boundary while preserving goodness.
Luqman teaches his son that even a hidden mustard-seed deed is brought forth by God; this is a concrete lesson shaping a child's moral understanding.
Luqman teaches his son prayer, urging good, forbidding wrong, and patience; this is explicit moral upbringing through instruction.
The father teaches his son not to turn away from people or walk arrogantly; this continues the parent's formation of conduct.
The father teaches his son measured walking and a lowered voice; this completes a specific sequence of child-rearing through practical instruction.
Abraham and Jacob enjoin their sons to remain devoted to God; this is direct intergenerational instruction within a family.
Jacob asks his sons whom they will worship after him, and they answer with faith in one God; this continues the parental instruction in 2:132.
Abraham asks God to make him and his offspring steadfast in prayer; this makes spiritual formation of children a parent's explicit concern.
After the distinction between adopted sons and lineage in 33:4–5, this ayah states that blood relatives are closer to one another; it sharpens the section's womb-based kinship boundary.
The verse permits marriage to the former wife of an adopted son and explains the ruling; it continues 33:4–5 by distinguishing foster status from biological lineage.
The verse says the Prophet is not the father of any of the men; in this passage on adoption, it marks the boundary between household care and biological fatherhood.
The command to read in the name of the Lord who created begins the passage where teaching by the pen follows in 96:4–5; this frames learning as part of divine formation.
The repeated command to read names the Lord as most generous; the following ayat describe teaching by pen and teaching what was unknown.
God teaches Adam the names; this is a specific scene of divine instruction that fits the section's extension of ر ب ب from nurture to teaching.
Abraham asks for a messenger who will teach the Book and wisdom; this is a specific model of instruction as a formative gift to a community.
The messenger's work includes teaching the Book and wisdom; this repeats the section's move from bodily upbringing to instruction.
God's favor to believers includes sending a messenger to teach the Book and wisdom; this is a specific communal form of the section's teaching-nurture image.
The messenger recites, purifies, and teaches the Book and wisdom; this is another explicit formulation of instruction as the growth of a community.
